facts.claim: UNESCO element 'Traditional tea processing techniques and associated social practices in China' is live; inscribed in 2022 (17.COM) on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.
facts.quote: Inscribed in 2022 (17.COM) on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity

facts.claim: The UNESCO tea element's text mentions weddings once: tea is part of socialisation and of ceremonies such as weddings. It does not describe a wedding tea ceremony or its steps; the page also carries a 'Wedding' keyword tag.
facts.quote: It is an important part of socialization and of ceremonies such as weddings and sacrifices.

facts.claim: The UNESCO tea element says greeting guests and building relationships within families through tea is common to multiple ethnic groups.
facts.quote: The practice of greeting guests and building relationships within families and among neighbours through tea-related activities is common to multiple ethnic groups

facts.claim: UNESCO element 'Chinese paper-cut' is live; inscribed in 2009 (4.COM) on the Representative List; its text lists weddings among festivities paper-cuts are made for.
facts.quote: which might be used for interior decor (windows, beds and ceilings), festivities (weddings, birthdays and ceremonies), or prayers
facts.region: China (throughout China and in various ethnic groups)

facts.claim: Smartraveller China: overall level is 'Exercise a high degree of caution', updated 28 September 2026, still current at 6 November 2026.
facts.quote: Still current at:06 November 2026Updated:28 September 2026 ... Exercise a high degree of caution in China overall. Higher levels apply in some areas.

facts.claim: Smartraveller China: reconsider your need to travel to Gyirong County in Tibet (flooding and landslides); high degree of caution in Tibet and Xinjiang.
facts.quote: Reconsider your need to travel to Gyirong County, in Tibet, China, due to the ongoing risk of severe flooding and landslides. ... Exercise a high degree of caution in Tibet and Xinjiang due to the security situation and associated measures.

facts.claim: Smartraveller China: Australia is in China's visa waiver program until 31 December 2026; ordinary passport holders may be able to enter visa-free for no more than 30 days for business, tourism, visiting family and friends or transit; an electronic arrival card is required.
facts.quote: China has included Australia in its visa waiver program effective until 31 December 2026. If you hold an ordinary Australian passport, you may be able to enter China without a visa for no more than 30 days for business, tourism, visiting family and friends or transit. ... You must complete an electronic arrival card to enter China.

facts.claim: Smartraveller China: China does not recognise dual nationality; dual nationals who don't enter on their Australian passport may be unable to access Australian consular services. Also: Australians may be at risk of arbitrary detention, exit bans or harsh enforcement of local laws, including broadly defined National Security Laws.
facts.quote: This includes if you're a dual national and don't enter China on your Australian passport. ... Australians may be at risk of arbitrary detention, exit bans or harsh enforcement of local laws, including broadly defined National Security Laws

facts.claim: Smartraveller 'Getting married overseas' (last updated 18/08/2026): you can't register an overseas marriage in Australia, but in most cases it is legally recognised if valid where it happened and valid under Australian law had it occurred in Australia; talk to a lawyer to confirm.
facts.quote: You can't register an overseas marriage in Australia. But in most cases, your marriage is legally recognised here. ... valid under the law of the country where it happened; valid under Australian law if it had occurred in Australia.

facts.claim: Smartraveller 'Getting married overseas': some countries ask for proof you are free to marry (commonly a CNI or registry certificates); contact the destination's embassy or consulate for specific details.
facts.quote: We can't tell you what you will need. Find out the laws about marriage where you're going. ... Contact your destination's embassy or consulate for specific details.

facts.claim: Smartraveller CNI page (last updated 01/10/2026): DFAT issues CNIs through Australian Passport Offices, Australian embassies/consulates overseas, or by mail; fees apply (no amounts recorded); some authorities only accept a CNI issued in their country, in which case the Australian embassy or consulate there can issue it.
facts.quote: DFAT issues CNIs: through Australian Passport Offices across Australia; through Australian embassies, high commissions, and consulates overseas; by mail. ... Note that we charge fees for our service.

facts.claim: Australian Embassy in China website is live at china.embassy.gov.au (address 21 Dongzhimenwai Street, Chaoyang District, Beijing). The home page read does not describe CNI or notarial services for marriage in China; Consulates-General Shanghai, Guangzhou and Chengdu URLs are from the stage 02 Smartraveller notes, not re-read.
facts.quote: Welcome to the website of the Australian Embassy in China ... 21 Dongzhimenwai Street, Chaoyang District, Beijing

facts.claim: V&A: red is the primary colour for traditional Chinese wedding ceremonies.
facts.quote: Red is the primary colour for traditional Chinese wedding ceremonies.
facts.region: Chinese weddings (general); object made in Hong Kong, 1940-1970

facts.claim: V&A: the bride's matching red jacket and skirt is known as hong gua ('red gown'), sometimes 'qun kwa', and its design is still predominated by the dragon and phoenix, often in metal couched threads. The V&A does not tie the term to Cantonese brides specifically; the object was made and bought in Hong Kong.
facts.quote: what is more popularly known as "hong gua" (sometimes "qun kwa") which is a set of matching red jacket and skirt whose design is still predominated by the dragon and phoenix, often with the metal couched threads covering the whole of the satin.
facts.region: Chinese weddings (general); object made in Hong Kong, 1940-1970

facts.claim: V&A record: the dragon was said to represent the male and the phoenix the female; side by side they symbolise the balance of yin and yang of bride and groom (stated as 'was said', so the article attributes it).
facts.quote: dragon was said to represent the male and phoenix the female, having them side by side symbolises the perfect balance of yin and yang of the bride and the groom
facts.region: Chinese weddings (general); object made in Hong Kong, 1940-1970

facts.claim: V&A: today white wedding dresses are popular, but traditional bridal ensembles are still worn for rituals in front of parents and ancestors and during the wedding banquets.
facts.quote: Today, white wedding dresses are popular, but traditional bridal ensembles are still worn for the performing of rituals in front of parents and ancestors, and during the wedding banquets.
facts.region: Chinese weddings (general); object made in Hong Kong, 1940-1970

facts.claim: V&A (citing Valery Garrett, Chinese Clothing: An Illustrated Guide, 1994): over time ready-made wedding clothing was usually sent to the bride from the groom's family, and it became usual to hire these expensive outfits.
facts.quote: articles of ready-made wedding clothing were usually sent to the bride from the bridegroom's family, which were usually borrowed or rented for the occasion. ... It then became far more usual to hire these expensive outfits.
facts.region: Chinese weddings (general); object made in Hong Kong, 1940-1970

facts.claim: British Museum: lucky red envelopes are called 'hong bao' in Mandarin and 'lai see' in Cantonese; this pack was designed for making gifts of money at weddings.
facts.quote: Sealed pack of lucky red envelopes ['hong bao' in Mandarin; 'lai see' in Cantonese]. ... These envelopes were designed for making gifts of money at weddings.
facts.region: Hong Kong (object acquired in Hong Kong, 2001); Mandarin and Cantonese names given by the source

facts.claim: British Museum: the wedding envelopes carry the 'double happiness' character (shuang xi), used at weddings.
facts.quote: The inscription is the 'double happiness' character, used as weddings. ... This character is known as 'shuang xi' ... Inscription translation: Double Happiness
facts.region: Hong Kong (object acquired in Hong Kong, 2001); Mandarin and Cantonese names given by the source

insider_details.detail: As at November 2026, Australians on an ordinary passport may be able to enter China visa-free for up to 30 days under a waiver that runs to 31 December 2026, so a wedding trip after that date needs the visa position rechecked when booking.
Chinese-Australian dual nationals should travel on their Australian passport: China does not recognise dual nationality and consular help can be lost otherwise. Flag this early on the guest list.

A marriage in China can't be registered in Australia but is usually recognised if valid there and under Australian law; ask the Chinese authorities whether they need a CNI, whether it must be issued in China, and whether it needs legalising, then budget lead time for DFAT processing (fees apply).

Many brides change between a white gown and a red embroidered hong gua / qun kwa for family rituals and the banquet; the V&A notes these outfits were often hired, so build a fitting and hire slot into the plan.

Red envelopes printed with the double happiness character were made specifically for wedding money gifts; a guest table or box for them at the reception is worth planning, with no amounts suggested in copy.
